Q: How do protocol versions, negotiated capabilities and transport choices constrain MCP interoperability?
A: MCP interoperability depends on a shared protocol profile, supported capabilities and the chosen transport's lifecycle, not only a successful connection. Negotiate or verify the applicable version and expose unsupported operations clearly. Standard input/output is a local process transport, while remote HTTP introduces network, identity and authorization concerns. Tools, resources and prompts retain distinct semantics. A public read-only demonstration establishes a smaller contract than authenticated remote tool access, so state the tested profile and avoid inferring security properties from a client library name.
Why: A client can connect and list tools while not supporting an extension needed by one operation. Treat the operation as unsupported or adapt it deliberately instead of sending a request the peer cannot interpret safely.
Risk: Transport connectivity can be mistaken for complete protocol conformance.
Trade: Pin and test representative profiles while planning compatible version evolution.
Try: Test one negotiated capability and one explicitly unsupported operation across two transports.
